What we could not confirm

Who records deeds and mortgages in Orleans Parish?

The Land Records Division of the Clerk of Civil District Court for the Parish of Orleans records every deed, mortgage and judgment of possession for property in New Orleans. It sits at 1340 Poydras Street, 4th floor, New Orleans, LA 70112, and its phone number is (504) 407-0005.

Three offices used to do this work separately: the Recorder of Mortgages, the Register of Conveyances and the Custodian of Notarial Archives. The Legislature passed a consolidation law in 2006, it took effect on January 1, 2009, and the clerk finished merging the three indexes into one system on February 18, 2014. Today an owner or buyer files in one place, and a cover sheet tells the clerk whether the document goes into the mortgage records, the conveyance records, or both.

The clerk's history page says the Conveyance Office was founded in 1827, that the Recorder of Mortgages was first appointed in the 1760s, and that notarial documents in the archives go back as far as 1735.

OfficeAddressPhone
Land Records Division1340 Poydras Street, 4th Floor(504) 407-0005
Research Center and historical records1340 Poydras Street, Suite 360(504) 407-0106
Civil Division (court filings)421 Loyola Avenue, Room 402(504) 407-0000

All three are open Monday through Friday, 8:30 AM to 5:00 PM, and the Land Records office does not close for lunch. The clerk's hours page lists the details and legal holidays.

What does it cost to record a deed in Orleans Parish?

A deed of up to five pages costs $100 in the base recording fee, plus a $5 portal fee and a $30 building fund fee, so the listed parts add up to $135 before any extras. That sum is our own addition of the clerk's published line items, so confirm the total with the office before you send a check.

The base fee comes from La. R.S. 13:844 and rises with page count. If a document is recorded in both the mortgage and conveyance records, the clerk assesses the fee twice. The base fee already covers one certified copy and indexing of up to ten names.

ItemFee
Recording, 1 to 5 pages$100
Recording, 6 to 25 pages$200
Recording, 26 to 50 pages$300
Each page over 50$5 added to $300
Louisiana Clerks' Remote Access Authority portal fee$5 per recording
Courthouse building fund fee$30 per recording
Each name indexed after the first ten$5
Survey, sketch or blueprint$30

The fee sheet we read carries a March 2021 update date, while the clerk's FAQ was updated in August 2026. Treat the numbers as the posted schedule and ask the office whether anything has changed.

What paperwork rules can get a deed rejected?

The clerk can reject a document, or charge a $20 surcharge, when the page margins are too narrow for the bound record books. The first page needs a two inch margin at the top, and every page needs one inch at the bottom and on both sides. Type size cannot be smaller than eight point, and the first page must carry a caption naming the type of act.

Other rules that catch people out:

  • Paper other than 8.5 by 11 or 8.5 by 14 inches costs an extra $20 per page.
  • Attachments such as surveys, tax certificates and mortgage certificates count toward the page total.
  • The clerk keeps the original and does not return it, because recorded documents are bound into books.

Payment has its own limits. By mail, send a business check or money order payable to Clerk of Court. The office does not accept personal checks. In person, you can also pay with cash or a major credit card. eRecording is available through CSC, ePN and Simplifile, but cancellations, certificates, surveys and a few other document types cannot be filed that way.

What is the New Orleans documentary transaction tax?

It is a city tax charged on documents that transfer or create rights in property in Orleans Parish. The Notarial Archives collects it under contract with the city, and the clerk's page lists sales, donations, transfers, mortgages and commercial leases as taxable documents.

The flat amount is $325 per taxable document. Mortgages with a loan amount under $9,000 follow a smaller scale: $75 under $3,000, $125 from $3,000.01 to $6,000, and $175 from $6,000.01 to $9,000.

  • The seller, donor, mortgagor or commercial lessee is the party responsible for paying it.
  • It is paid when the document is recorded, or billed and paid within 30 days.
  • Late payment brings interest and a $500 penalty.
  • A taxable document that is not a single-family home or residential double and runs over 25 pages adds $100 per page, up to $2,525.
  • A single-family home or residential double over 25 pages stays at $325 if a notarized statement says it is owner occupied.

For an eRecorded sale, payment goes by check or money order to the City of New Orleans, with the recordation information written on it. The details are on the clerk's documentary tax page. Because the seller is the responsible party, sellers should look for this line on the closing statement.

How do you search Orleans Parish land records before a sale?

You can search for free at the clerk's public computers on the 3rd, 4th and 5th floors of 1340 Poydras Street, or remotely through a paid subscription. The searchable fields include names, municipal address, filing date, document type and legal description by District, Square and Lot.

IndexCoverage
Mortgage indexSeptember 21, 1987 through February 14, 2014
Conveyance indexJanuary 1, 1989 through February 14, 2014
Unified Indexing SystemFebruary 18, 2014 forward
Document imagesJanuary 1, 2005 forward (some from 1970 to 2004)

Online Records subscriptions cost $20 for 24 hours, $100 for a month or $700 for a year, and downloading or printing images needs a separate escrow account. The state portal eClerks LA is free and searches indexes for all 64 parishes at once.

Copies are $1 per page, and no ID is needed for a copy except a military discharge.

How are liens and mortgages cleared when you sell in Orleans Parish?

A paid-off mortgage comes off the record only when release paperwork from the lender is brought to the Land Records Division. Recording the cancellation costs $50, a Certificate of Cancellation is another $13, and the request cannot be filed electronically.

Buyers and title companies usually order a mortgage certificate before closing. The clerk's schedule lists $20 for the first name on a regular mortgage certificate and $10 for each added name, and $35 for the first name on a conveyance certificate with $30 for each added name. The FAQ says a mortgage certificate shows lien information for up to 30 years.

Contractor liens work on a timetable. A lien and privilege certificate cannot be requested until an Acceptance, Substantial Completion or Termination is recorded and the lien period has run, which is at least 30 days and can be longer if the contract says so. A seller with recent repair work done on the house should check for this before listing.

What is the deed called in Louisiana, and what does the law require?

The clerk calls the document that moves title an Act of Sale, and it can take the form of a Cash Sale, a Credit Sale or a Warranty Deed. Louisiana is a civil law state, so these terms differ from the grant deeds and quitclaim deeds used elsewhere.

Louisiana Civil Code art. 1839 says a transfer of immovable property must be made by authentic act or by an act under private signature. The same article makes the instrument effective against third persons only from the time it is filed for registry in the parish where the property sits, which is why recording at the Orleans clerk matters. La. R.S. 9:2721 also requires the deed to name the person responsible for property taxes and a mailing address for tax notices.

Judgments of possession are recorded in the same division as sales and mortgages.

What should New Orleans sellers know about recording when selling for cash?

A cash sale in Orleans Parish still ends at the Land Records Division, so the paperwork is the same whether the buyer is a family or an investor. The clerk's office can describe the filing steps but cannot give legal advice or say which documents to file.

  • Ask the closing office whether the deed will be eRecorded or hand delivered.
  • Ask who is paying the $325 documentary tax and where it appears on the settlement statement.
  • Order a mortgage certificate early so open liens surface before closing day.
  • Confirm any recorded cancellations were actually filed, using the mortgage instrument number and the Cancel Status field, where a C means fully cancelled and a P means partly cancelled.

If you inherited the house, are behind on payments or want to skip repairs, call us for a written offer and we will explain how the closing and recording would work on your property.

More questions about Orleans Parish, LA Clerk of Court

Where is the Orleans Parish clerk of court's land records office?

The Land Records Division is at 1340 Poydras Street, 4th floor, New Orleans, LA 70112. It is open Monday through Friday from 8:30 AM to 5:00 PM and does not close for lunch. The phone number is (504) 407-0005.

How much is the recording fee for a deed in Orleans Parish?

The base fee is $100 for one to five pages, $200 for six to 25 pages and $300 for 26 to 50 pages, plus $5 for each page over 50. A $5 portal fee and a $30 building fund fee are added to each recording. Extra charges apply for added addresses, squares, names and nonstandard paper.

Is there a transfer tax when you sell a house in New Orleans?

The city charges a documentary transaction tax of $325 on a sale, which the seller is responsible for paying. It is paid at recording or billed and due within 30 days, after which interest and a $500 penalty apply. It is separate from the recording fee.

Can I record a deed by mail or online in Orleans Parish?

Yes to both. You can mail the original with a business check or money order payable to Clerk of Court, or use an eRecording vendor such as CSC, ePN or Simplifile. Personal checks and fax filings are not accepted for deeds.

How do I remove a paid-off mortgage from the record in Orleans Parish?

Bring the lender's release paperwork to the Land Records Division at 1340 Poydras Street. Cancelling a single mortgage costs $50, and an optional Certificate of Cancellation costs $13 more. Cancellations cannot be submitted by eRecording.

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Terrebonne Parish, LA Clerk of Court sale
  • Turn the Terrebonne Parish, LA Clerk of Court offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling in Terrebonne Parish? Get a Cash Offer

We buy Terrebonne Parish houses as-is and reply with a written cash offer.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What we confirmed on the official page

  • Recording fee schedule (revised 8/1/2017 PDF): 1-5 pages $105, 6-25 $205, 26-50 $305 (from the parish site listing; confirm with the office)

Fees

Selling in Terrebonne Parish?
We buy Terrebonne Parish houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What we could not confirm

Where is the Terrebonne Parish Clerk of Court and what does it record?

The Terrebonne Parish Clerk of Court main office is at 7856 Main Street in Houma, and it keeps the conveyance and mortgage records for the parish. The office is open 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Monday through Friday, and the main phone is 985-868-5660.

The mailing address is PO Box 1569, Houma, LA 70361-1569. Some services are in other buildings, so check before you drive.

ServiceLocation
Main office, recording7856 Main Street, Houma
Birth, death and marriage records, appeals310 Church Street, Houma
Elections, jury, passports by appointment415 Goode Street, Houma

The clerk's site lists separate departments for conveyance, mortgage, recording, indexing and maps, which shows how many steps a deed passes through.

How do you record a deed in Terrebonne Parish?

You record a deed by filing the notarized act of sale with the clerk, either in person or through e-recording on ClerkConnect. Louisiana law requires the transfer to be made by authentic act or act under private signature, and it binds third persons only once it is filed in the conveyance records of the parish where the house stands.

In practice the closing notary or title company usually files for you. Still, the act needs to be right:

  • name the buyer and seller as they appear in the earlier title;
  • include a legal description of the property;
  • designate the person responsible for property taxes and an address for notices, as La. R.S. 9:2721 requires.

The statute adds that anyone who acquires immovable property that is subject to a lease recorded earlier takes the property subject to it. A seller with a recorded lease should say so to the buyer.

What does it cost to record a deed in Terrebonne Parish?

The clerk's recording fee schedule, last revised August 1, 2017, starts at $105 for one to five pages in one index type. Documents of 6 to 25 pages are $205, and 26 to 50 pages are $305, each per recording book.

The clerk's schedule counts pages, so a short deed costs less to file than a long package. Ask whether extra pages such as exhibits or a legal description attachment change the page count.

We found the schedule on the clerk's own site, but it is dated, so ask the office to confirm the fee before you send a check. We did not find a state transfer tax figure on an official page we opened, so we state none. Ask your notary or title company what applies to your closing.

How can you search Terrebonne land records online?

You can search for free through the Louisiana Clerks of Court portal at eclerksla.com, and the Terrebonne clerk also runs its own eSearch. The clerk's site says the free statewide search covers land, civil, criminal and marriage records from participating parishes.

The clerk's eSearch account page mentions a $10.00 fee for some uses and accepts prepayments from $1 to $1,000. Search it before listing to look for old mortgages, liens or an earlier sale that was never cleared.

The clerk also promotes eClerks Alerts, a free service that notifies you when a document bearing your registered name is recorded in any parish. Owners of a vacant or inherited house in Terrebonne Parish may find it useful, because it can flag a fraudulent filing.

What is Terrebonne Parish like for a seller?

Terrebonne Parish is a Gulf Coast parish created on March 22, 1822, with Houma as parish seat and largest city. It has 1,232 square miles of land and 850 of water, and the 2020 census counted 109,580 people, with a 2025 estimate of 104,163.

Oil and gas development began in 1929, and the parish produces more than 20% of Louisiana's seafood, according to Wikipedia. Houma's elevation is about 10 feet, and Wikipedia notes extensive flood protection works.

Hurricane Ida struck Houma as a Category 4 storm on August 29, 2021, and Hurricane Francine made landfall in the parish on September 11, 2024. Storm damage, roof repairs and insurance claims are common themes in local house sales, and a buyer will ask for proof of past repairs.

The Terrebonne Parish Consolidated Government runs the parish, and Houma's city government was consolidated into it in 1984.

Which communities does the Terrebonne clerk serve?

The clerk records for the whole parish, from downtown Houma to the bayou communities in the south. Wikipedia names Bayou Cane, Montegut, Dulac, Chauvin, Dularge, Gibson and Pointe-au-Chien among the places in the parish.

Houma's downtown is a National Register historic district, and Bayou Cane is the largest unincorporated area next to the city. The Terrebonne Parish School District covers the entire parish, and the parish library system has eight branches.

Waterways shaped the settlement pattern. The Intracoastal Waterway dates from 1923, and the Houma Navigational Canal, completed in 1961, is a 30-mile link to Terrebonne Bay and the Gulf. A railroad from Schriever to Houma was built in 1872.

For a seller, this matters because a legal description of a bayou-side lot can be longer or more complicated than a subdivision lot in town. Surveys, servitudes and old family transfers sometimes appear in the chain of title.

How do inherited and family-held houses get recorded in Terrebonne Parish?

A house passed through a death often needs a succession handled first, and the clerk of court keeps both the civil records and the land records. Louisiana's rule that a transfer must be made by authentic act or act under private signature still applies after that, so the heirs sign the act of sale like any other owner.

The clerk's site lists civil records and civil processing alongside conveyance and mortgage, so one office holds the whole trail. If the succession was never opened, expect extra time and cost, and plan for that before you set a closing date.

  • Search the land records for the last recorded transfer into the family.
  • Check the civil records for an open or closed succession.
  • Find out whether any heir lives out of state and needs to sign remotely.

The statewide eClerks search is helpful for relatives who live elsewhere in Louisiana and want to see what is recorded without a trip to Houma.

What should you check before closing a Terrebonne sale?

Before closing, confirm that the title is clean, the taxes are current and the act of sale matches the recorded chain of title. A mortgage certificate shows liens, and the clerk's mortgage department issues them.

  • Get a payoff for any mortgage and confirm how it will be cancelled in the records.
  • Ask the parish tax collector for a tax payoff at 985-857-0230.
  • Check for a succession if an owner has died, since a deed needs someone with authority to sign.
  • Confirm whether a recorded lease binds the buyer.

For a cash sale, the same filings apply. The buyer or the title company can e-record the day of closing, so ownership shows up in the public record quickly.

More questions about Terrebonne Parish, LA Clerk of Court

Where do I record a deed in Terrebonne Parish?

You record it with the Terrebonne Parish Clerk of Court at 7856 Main Street, Houma, or through e-recording on ClerkConnect.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Terrebonne Parish?

The clerk's schedule revised August 1, 2017 lists $105 for one to five pages, $205 for 6 to 25 and $305 for 26 to 50. Confirm with the office because the schedule is dated.

Is there a transfer tax in Terrebonne Parish?

We could not confirm one on an official page, so we do not state a figure. Ask the clerk or your closing notary.

Can I search Terrebonne property records for free?

Yes. The Louisiana Clerks of Court portal offers a free statewide search of land, civil, criminal and marriage records.

What must a Louisiana deed say about taxes?

It must name the person responsible for property taxes and give an address for tax notices, under La. R.S. 9:2721.

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Jefferson Parish, LA Clerk of Court sale
  • Turn the Jefferson Parish, LA Clerk of Court offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling in Jefferson Parish? Get a Cash Offer

We buy Jefferson Parish houses as-is and reply with a written cash offer.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What we confirmed on the official page

  • Fees page: document recording 1-5 pages $105.00 (6-25 amount truncated) (from the parish site listing; confirm with the office)

Fees

Selling in Jefferson Parish?
We buy Jefferson Parish houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What we could not confirm

  • Jefferson BOR appeal deadline not found

Is there a Jefferson County clerk of court in Louisiana?

Louisiana has parishes instead of counties, so the office people search for as the Jefferson County clerk of court is the Jefferson Parish Clerk of Court, based in Gretna. The Clerk's website describes its Mortgage and Conveyance department as the keeper of the parish's official public land records, which is where a house sale ends up on paper.

The Clerk also runs the 24th Judicial District Court records, the First and Second Parish Courts and the Juvenile Court records. For a seller, the land records office is the one that matters on closing day.

Where is Jefferson Parish, and what does that mean for a seller?

Jefferson Parish is a large suburban parish next to New Orleans, split by the Mississippi River into an East Bank and a West Bank. According to Wikipedia, the 2020 census counted 440,781 residents. Gretna is the parish seat, Metairie is the largest community, and Kenner is the largest incorporated city.

The parish measures 665 square miles in total, but only 296 of them are land because Lake Pontchartrain borders the north and much of the southern half is marsh. Grand Isle is reached only by roads that run through Lafourche and St. Charles parishes. The legislature created the parish in 1825 and set its current border with Orleans Parish in 1874, when the parish seat moved to Gretna.

TypePlaces in Jefferson Parish
CitiesGretna (parish seat), Harahan, Kenner, Westwego
TownsGrand Isle, Jean Lafitte
Largest unincorporated communityMetairie
Other named communitiesAvondale, Bridge City, Harvey, Marrero, River Ridge, Terrytown, Waggaman and more

The Clerk's land records sit on the West Bank in Gretna. A seller in Metairie or Kenner who wants to look at records in person has to cross the river, which is one reason the e-recording system described below matters.

Where does the Jefferson Parish clerk record a deed?

Deeds and other real estate documents are recorded by the Mortgage and Conveyance/UCC department in the Jefferson Parish General Government Building, 200 Derbigny Street, Suite 2200, Gretna, LA 70053. The office is open Monday to Friday from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM, excluding legal holidays. The mailing address is P.O. Box 10, Gretna, LA 70054-0010.

  • General information on prices and copies: (504) 364-2943 or (504) 364-2944.
  • Certificates and UCC research: (504) 364-2954.
  • Mortgage cancellations: (504) 364-2963.
  • Email: mortgageinfo@jeffparishclerk.gov.

The Clerk lists several kinds of documents it records for the parish: real estate transfers and acts of sale, mortgages, liens and judgments, military discharges, corporation charters, trade name affidavits, and oil, gas and mineral lease transfers. The East Bank office in the Joseph S. Yenni Building handles marriage licenses, passports and elections, and does not list land records among its services.

How soon must a Jefferson Parish act of sale be recorded?

Louisiana law gives a notary 15 days to record a sale of land outside Orleans Parish. Under R.S. 35:199, notaries must record acts of sale, exchange, donation and mortgage of immovable property that pass before them, and for property outside the parish of Orleans they must file with the proper parish recorder within fifteen days.

In practice, a Louisiana sale is signed before a notary at closing, and the title company or the closing attorney sends the act to the Clerk. Because the statute puts the duty on the notary, the closing agent normally handles the filing, and the seller's part is to provide a correct legal description and signed documents.

What does it cost to record a deed in Jefferson Parish?

Recording a document of 1 to 5 pages costs $105 at the Jefferson Parish Clerk. The Clerk's fee page sets mortgage and conveyance fees under R.S. 13:844 and says the office receives no ad valorem tax funding, so its operations are paid by fees set by the Legislature.

Document recordingFee
1 to 5 pages$105.00
6 to 25 pages$205.00
26 to 50 pages$305.00
51 pages or more$305.00 for the first 50 pages, then $5.00 per page

The base fee covers all parts of the act and its attachments, such as exhibits, powers of attorney, property descriptions, tax certificates and surveys. It includes one certified copy and indexing of up to ten names. Further names cost $5.00 each, pages larger than 8.5 by 14 inches add $20.00 per page, and the fee is charged once for each book designation, so a document recorded as both a conveyance and a mortgage costs double.

Since August 1, 2018, every recording also carries a $5.00 fee under R.S. 13:754 that supports the statewide LCRAA system, charged once per instrument.

Is there a transfer tax on a Jefferson Parish sale?

The Clerk's fee schedule shows no transfer tax line. What it lists for a sale is the recording charge, any certificates ordered, and the optional extras that closing agents add. Confirm with your closing attorney or title company, who prepare the settlement statement, since they know what applies to a given deal.

The costs that do appear on the Clerk's page are these:

  • Mortgage or lien and privilege certificate: $20.00 for the first name and $10.00 for each additional name; $40.00 more if clerk staff prepare it.
  • Act or affidavit to cancel a single mortgage, lien or privilege: $55.00.
  • Release of a mortgage with the original paraphed note: $10.00 per mortgage; a Notice of Cancellation adds $10.00 per mortgage inscription released.
  • Copies: $1.00 per page uncertified, and $10.00 per document certified plus copy costs for mortgage records.

Since April 7, 2017, the Clerk has contracted with Jefferson Certificate Corp. in Gretna to prepare mortgage and conveyance certificates. The Clerk's page gives (504) 361-0206 for ordinary acts of sale or mortgage.

Can I record a Jefferson Parish deed online?

Yes. The Clerk accepts mortgage and conveyance documents, including requests to cancel mortgage inscriptions, through JeffNet, its secure online records system. The system gives 24-hour access to property, civil, criminal and other public records.

JeffNet optionPriceWhat it includes
24-hour access$5.00Online access to records; certified copies at $0.75 per page plus a $10.00 certification fee for mortgage records
Monthly subscription$50.00 per user IDE-filing and e-recording, available to all monthly subscribers and not limited to attorneys

Because e-recording is open to all monthly subscribers, a closing agent can file a sale without a trip to Gretna. A seller can use the 24-hour option to look up the recorded mortgage on the house.

Which Jefferson Parish clerk filings matter to sellers with estate or foreclosure problems?

Two clerk filings commonly come up for sellers who cannot close cleanly: a succession for an inherited house, and executory process, which is Louisiana's foreclosure suit. The civil fee table lists advance deposits for both.

Filing in the 24th JDCAdvance deposit
Succession under $125,000 (La. C.C.P. Art. 3422)$200.00
Succession of $125,000 and over$400.00
Executory process (foreclosure)$1,000.00
Judicial eviction trial in a Parish Court$375.00 plus a bond set by the court

The page calls these a guide and says the actual charge can vary. A succession is the court filing used to settle a deceased owner's estate, which is why it comes up for inherited houses in Gretna, Marrero, Kenner and elsewhere in the parish. The 24th JDC civil records are at 200 Derbigny Street, Suite 2400, in the same complex as the land records office.

More questions about Jefferson Parish, LA Clerk of Court

Where do I record a deed in Jefferson Parish?

Deeds are recorded by the Mortgage and Conveyance/UCC department of the Jefferson Parish Clerk of Court, at 200 Derbigny Street, Suite 2200, Gretna, LA 70053. It is open weekdays from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Jefferson Parish?

The fee is $105.00 for 1 to 5 pages, $205.00 for 6 to 25 pages and $305.00 for 26 to 50 pages, plus $5.00 per page beyond 50. A $5.00 LCRAA fee also applies to each recording.

Does the Jefferson Parish Clerk list a transfer tax?

Its fee schedule has no transfer tax line. Ask the closing attorney or title company what appears on your settlement statement.

Can my title company e-record a Jefferson Parish deed?

Yes, through JeffNet. E-recording is available to all monthly subscribers at $50.00 per user ID, not only to attorneys.

How long does a notary have to record a sale in Jefferson Parish?

Fifteen days. R.S. 35:199 requires notaries to record sales of immovable property outside Orleans Parish with the parish recorder within fifteen days after the act is passed.

What do I need to sell an inherited house in Jefferson Parish?

A succession is the court filing for settling a deceased owner's estate. The Clerk lists an advance deposit of $200.00 for a succession under $125,000 and $400.00 for larger ones, and says actual costs may vary.

Lafayette Parish, LA Clerk of Court: Recording a Deed, Fees and Transfer Tax

Cash Home Buyers in Louisiana

What we could not confirm

  • Lafayette BOR appeal deadline not found

What does the Lafayette Parish Clerk of Court do with a deed?

The clerk records the deed, which is how a Louisiana property sale becomes effective against everyone outside the contract. Under Civil Code article 3338, a written instrument that transfers an immovable has no effect as to a third person until it is recorded in the conveyance records.

Lafayette Parish's clerk, Louis J. Perret, serves the 15th Judicial District and acts as the ex-officio recorder. The Recording Department files conveyance, mortgage and UCC documents deposited in the parish. When a document is presented, it receives an entry number with the date, hour and minute of filing, and a short description and the first parties appear on the clerk's online records search right away.

The clerk reports that about two to three hundred documents are filed each day, and that full indexing with all party names is complete by the following day.

What are the recording fees for a Lafayette Parish deed?

A conveyance or mortgage of one to five pages costs $105 to record in a single index type. The clerk's schedule includes the $5 statewide portal fee, up to ten names indexed and one certified copy in each price.

Document lengthOne book (conveyance or mortgage)Both books
1 to 5 pages$105$205
6 to 25 pages$205$405
26 to 50 pages$305$605
51 pages or more$305 plus $5 per extra page$605 plus $5 per extra page

The two-book column applies when one document goes into both records, and the fees are assessed separately for each book, except for the single $5 portal charge. The schedule also lists $5 for each name after the tenth, $20 per page for paper other than 8.5 by 11 or 8.5 by 14 inches, and $25 per debtor on a judgment with no Social Security or tax ID number.

Is there a new recording charge coming in 2027?

Yes. The clerk's fee page announces that, effective January 1, 2027, Act 446 of the 2026 Regular Legislative Session adds $5 to every recorded document. A closing set for late December 2026 and one set for early January 2027 can therefore carry different recording totals.

The existing $5 portal fee dates from Act 173 of 2017, effective August 1, 2018. It funds the Louisiana Clerks Remote Access Authority, a state entity that runs a statewide portal for remote access to parish land records. Both charges are in addition to the page-based fee, so ask the closing office for the total before the closing date.

What other charges might appear at a Lafayette Parish closing?

Several smaller line items show up around the main recording fee, and the clerk's schedule lists them plainly.

  • Cancellation or partial release of a single mortgage, lien or privilege: $55.
  • Cancellation with the original paraphed note: $15.
  • Real estate mortgage certificate: $20 for the first name, $10 for each additional name, and $15 for each additional property.
  • Non-lien certificate: $20 per name.
  • Copies: $1 per page in the office, $10 plus the copy fee for a certified copy, and $5 plus the copy fee for a conformed copy.

A mortgage certificate lists the recorded mortgages and privileges that stand against a seller's name. Title agents order it to confirm that every lien is paid and cancelled before the buyer's money is released.

How are documents prepared and submitted in Lafayette Parish?

The clerk wants every document to carry a caption identifying the type of act on its first page, with a 2 inch margin at the top and 1 inch at the bottom and sides, and type no smaller than 8 point. Paper can be 8.5 by 11 or 8.5 by 14 inches, and the clerk cites R.S. 13:844(B) for these rules.

A single document counts as all the pages presented together, including exhibits, riders, powers of attorney, property descriptions, tax certificates, surveys and mortgage certificates. That matters for the price, because the page count determines the tier.

Electronic recording is encouraged. The clerk's home page links three e-recording platforms, CSC, ePN and Simplifile, and most title companies already use one of them. If you mail a paper act, enclose a self-addressed stamped envelope or the postage is charged at actual cost.

Does the clerk return original documents?

No. The clerk states that, unlike most other states, original documents sent to the Clerk of the District Court and Ex-Officio Recorder are not returned. They become part of the parish archives.

What a filer can get back is a certified copy. It can be requested at the time of filing from the Recording Department, or later from the Land Records and Copy Department. A seller who needs proof of the sale for the Assessor or a lender should order that copy during closing.

Cancellations follow a separate path. They go first to the Cancellation Clerk in the Recording Department for verification, and in Lafayette Parish they must be in authentic form, executed before a notary public and signed by the affiant. UCC terminations use a Louisiana-approved form and can be sent directly.

How can you search Lafayette Parish land records?

The clerk's online records search covers mortgage, conveyance and UCC records, and the free eClerks LA portal indexes land, civil, marriage and probate records across Louisiana. A free alert service on eClerks LA monitors land records across parishes.

Paid land records access, including document images, is sold as a subscription: $20 for one day, $50 for 30 days or $600 for 365 days, with a $1 per page printing fee. Searching the index for liens under a seller's name before listing can show a forgotten mortgage or judgment that would otherwise appear at closing.

The clerk's home page notes that filings may become public record under the Public Records Act, and it lists items prohibited in the courthouse, including cellphones, cameras and recording devices. Bring paper documents and a printed list of the numbers you need rather than relying on a phone.

You can reach the clerk at 800 S. Buchanan St., Lafayette, LA 70501, or by mail at P.O. Box 2009, Lafayette, LA 70502. The main number is (337) 291-6400, and the Recording Department is at (337) 291-6310.

What should a seller confirm before the deed is recorded?

Confirm that property taxes are paid, because Louisiana lets any party to a conveyance of real property outside New Orleans obtain a certificate showing whether state, parish, municipal and levee district taxes have been paid, other than those for the year of the sale (R.S. 9:2901).

  • Ask for the tax certificate and for a mortgage certificate on every owner's name.
  • Check that any prior mortgage has a cancellation ready to record.
  • Ask the closing office whether the recording date falls before or after January 1, 2027.
  • Request a certified copy of the recorded act for your own file.

A seller who plans to take a cash offer should review the same list, since the buyer's title agent will run these searches before funding. Surprises are easier to fix before the closing day than after.

More questions about Lafayette Parish, LA Clerk of Court

How much does it cost to record a deed in Lafayette Parish?

A one to five page conveyance in a single book costs $105, which includes a $5 portal fee, ten indexed names and one certified copy. Six to 25 pages costs $205.

Is there a transfer tax charge on the Lafayette Parish fee schedule?

The fee schedule we opened lists recording, cancellation, copy and certificate fees but no transfer tax line. Ask your closing agent for the full settlement figures.

Does the Lafayette Parish clerk return my original deed?

No. Originals become part of the parish archives. You can obtain a certified copy at filing or later from the Land Records and Copy Department.

Can I e-record a deed in Lafayette Parish?

Yes, and the clerk encourages it. The clerk's site links to CSC, ePN and Simplifile for electronic recording of mortgage, conveyance and UCC documents.

What changes on January 1, 2027?

Act 446 of the 2026 Regular Legislative Session adds $5 to every recorded document starting that date, according to the clerk's fee page.

Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Livingston Parish, LA Clerk of Court: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Livingston Parish, LA Clerk of Court sale
  • Turn the Livingston Parish, LA Clerk of Court offer down and you owe us nothing

We buy Livingston Parish houses as-is and reply with a written cash offer.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Livingston Parish?
We buy Livingston Parish houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

  • Clerk address/hours not seen
  • Sheriff interest text from news article only

What does the Livingston Parish Clerk of Court do when a house sells?

The clerk is the parish recorder: deeds, mortgages and other property papers become public record at the clerk's recording desk. Louisiana counties are called parishes, and in Livingston Parish that office is the one buyers, sellers, title companies and heirs all end up dealing with.

When a document arrives, a deputy clerk stamps it with a unique instrument number and an index book and page number. The stamp also records the date, hour and minute of filing.

Under Civil Code article 3346, an instrument that creates or relates to a mortgage or privilege on land goes into the mortgage records of the parish. Every other instrument, including an act of sale, goes into the conveyance records. A single closing in Livingston Parish can therefore put papers into both sets of books.

Where is the Livingston Parish Clerk of Court office and when is it open?

The main office is at 20300 Government Blvd., Livingston, LA 70754, with a mailing address of P. O. Box 1150. The phone number listed on the clerk's locations page is 225-686-2216 and the fax is 225-686-1867.

A satellite office is listed in Denham Springs at 145 Del Orleans Avenue, Bldg. 2, Suite E, 70726. We could not confirm which services, including recording, are handled at the satellite, so call before driving there with a deed.

The hours page gives office hours as Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Closings that fall near these dates should be planned around the holiday list for 2026:

  • Tuesday, November 3 (General Election Day)
  • Wednesday, November 11 (Veterans' Day)
  • Thursday and Friday, November 26 and 27 (Thanksgiving and the day after)
  • Thursday, December 24, Friday, December 25 and Thursday, December 31

How much does it cost to record a deed in Livingston Parish?

Recording a deed or mortgage of one to five pages costs $125 under the clerk's posted schedule. Longer documents cost more, and a few extras apply to indexing and to papers that are formatted wrongly.

ItemFee on the clerk's schedule
Recording, pages 1 to 5$125.00
Recording, pages 6 to 25$225.00
Recording, pages 26 to 50$325.00
Indexing, first ten names per bookIncluded
Each additional name per book$5
Copies, per page$1.00
Certified copy$10.00
Conformed copy$5.00
Cancellation of mortgage, original note$35.00
Cancellation with affidavit$75.00

These figures come from the fee page, which the clerk's site last modified in December 2025. Confirm the current total with the office before closing, because a legislature or a clerk can change a schedule at any time.

Is there a transfer tax when a house is recorded in Livingston Parish?

The clerk's fee schedule shows recording, indexing, copy, map and cancellation charges, and it lists no per-dollar transfer tax line. We could not find a separate parish transfer tax on the clerk's pages, so treat the schedule above as the clerk's side of the cost and ask the closing attorney or title company for the full settlement figures.

The distinction matters to sellers who expect a percentage-based charge at the clerk's counter. What the clerk collects is a fee for handling pages and names. Other closing items, such as payoff of a mortgage or unpaid property tax, are handled between the parties and the title company.

What format must a deed follow so the Livingston clerk will accept it cleanly?

The recording desk says Louisiana statutes set the format, and a document that misses it can draw an extra $10 noncompliance fee. The clerk quotes R.S. 13:844(D)(1): the document must be captioned by type of act on the first page, with a two inch margin at the top, a one inch margin at the bottom and sides, and type no smaller than eight point.

Multiple indebtedness mortgages carry the same format rule under R.S. 9:5217(B). A short checklist before sending a deed to the clerk:

  • Caption the first page with the type of act.
  • Leave the margins described above.
  • Use type of eight point or larger.
  • Do not expect the original back, because the clerk's page states that originals are not returned and become part of the parish archives.

If you want proof of what you filed, the filing party can ask for a certified copy with the clerk's endorsement at the time of filing.

How do mortgage certificates and mortgage cancellations work here?

The mortgage section issues certificates and cancels mortgage inscriptions, and both start with a written request. Louisiana law requires certificate requests to be in writing, and the office accepts them by fax as well. You must name the exact people to check and supply a legal property description.

The clerk is careful to say a mortgage certificate, properly called a certificate of non-mortgage, is not a title opinion and says nothing about who owns the property. It lists what is recorded against the names searched.

On cancellations, the clerk's page states that since July 1, 2006, a borrower who pays off a mortgage on Livingston Parish real estate is responsible for making sure the mortgage is cancelled. The office requires the original note marked "paid" on its face and will not accept faxes or copies. If the note was lost, the page points the owner back to the lender, and it explains that lost note affidavits have mostly been replaced under R.S. 44:109 by an authentic act from a licensed financial institution.

For a seller, an old mortgage that was paid years ago but never cancelled can surface late in a sale. Checking the mortgage records early gives time to fix it.

How can a seller research a Livingston Parish property's records?

The conveyance section lets the public research property transactions, mineral leases, restrictions and subdivision maps through written or computerized indexes that date back to 1875. Large-screen computer stations are available for real estate agents, surveyors, appraisers, abstractors and attorneys, and staff help is free.

Surveys are a common stumbling block. The clerk notes Louisiana law does not require a survey of conveyed property to be recorded or separately indexed, so some surveys were never recorded or cannot be retrieved. The mapping section keeps a map index showing for whom a map was prepared, the property size, its location and the surveyor, and staff say a surveyor may hold a copy when the clerk does not.

For ownership lines, the clerk points to the parish ownership map on the assessor's website, livingstonassessor.com.

What is Livingston Parish like for a home seller?

Livingston Parish sits east of Baton Rouge, and the Greater Baton Rouge Economic Partnership profile lists Denham Springs, Walker, Livingston, Albany and Springfield as its cities and towns. Wikipedia's list adds Watson as an unincorporated census-designated place and names Livingston as the parish seat, so the main clerk's office sits in the town of Livingston.

The same profile calls it one of the fastest-growing parishes in Louisiana, with an annualized growth rate of 1.64 percent, and credits Interstate 12 for east-west access. It describes construction, distribution and retail as the parish's well-known sectors, and it names Northshore Technical Community College and Livingston Parish Public Schools as workforce and education anchors. The profile says the school district earned an "A" rating from the Louisiana Department of Education.

Watson, in the northwest part of the parish, sits around Range Road (LA 16) and Springfield Road (LA 1019), about 6 miles north of Denham Springs along LA 16.

How did the 2016 flood change selling a house in Livingston Parish?

The August 2016 flood is still part of nearly every house conversation in the parish. A state economic impact report estimated that 38,300 of Livingston Parish's 52,104 housing units flooded, and named East Baton Rouge and Livingston as the hardest hit parishes. The National Weather Service gauge page for the Amite River at Denham Springs lists August 14, 2016 as the flood of record.

For sellers this shows up in three ways:

  • Buyers and lenders ask whether a house took water, what was rebuilt and who did the work.
  • Elevation, flood zone and insurance history become part of price talks.
  • Records of repairs, permits and contractor payments help answer those questions.

A flood-history house that still needs work is a common reason owners look at an as-is sale instead of a repair and listing route.

What should heirs or owners with a distressed Livingston Parish house check first?

Start with the recorded history: pull the conveyance records for the last transfer, then the mortgage records for open liens. A clean record of who owns the house and what is owed makes any sale, cash or otherwise, move faster.

If the owner died, the paperwork that moves title to heirs is a court or affidavit process described on our Louisiana estate tax guide, and it ends with a document that eventually goes to the same recording desk. For rented houses, see our guides on the eviction process and the eviction notice.

More questions about Livingston Parish, LA Clerk of Court

Where do I record a deed in Livingston Parish?

At the Livingston Parish Clerk of Court's recording desk, 20300 Government Blvd., Livingston, LA 70754. A Denham Springs satellite office is also listed, but confirm by phone that it takes recordings. The main number is 225-686-2216.

How much is the recording fee for a short deed in Livingston Parish?

The clerk's schedule lists $125 for pages 1 to 5, $225 for pages 6 to 25 and $325 for pages 26 to 50, with the first ten names per book included in indexing. Check with the office for the current total.

Does the Livingston Parish clerk return the original deed?

No. The clerk's page says original documents are not returned and become part of the parish archives. You can request a certified copy with the clerk's endorsement at filing.

Who cancels a paid-off mortgage in Livingston Parish?

The borrower is responsible. The clerk says that since July 1, 2006, it is the borrower, not the lender, who may be hurt if a paid mortgage is not cancelled, and the office needs the original note marked paid.

Is a mortgage certificate the same as a title opinion?

No. The clerk states that a certificate of non-mortgage is not a title opinion and makes no representation about who owns the property.

Can I sell a flood-damaged Livingston Parish house as-is?

Yes, owners can sell as-is, but expect buyers to ask for repair, permit and insurance history. Get your recorded title and mortgage payoff in order first so the record does not slow the sale.

What does the Ouachita Parish Clerk of Court do for a home sale?

The Ouachita Parish Clerk of Court keeps the public land records for the parish, so a deed, mortgage or mortgage cancellation for a Monroe or West Monroe house is filed there. The clerk's recording department is the office that your closing attorney or title company deals with after you sign.

The clerk's website describes a wider office. Besides land records it handles civil and criminal filings, marriage licenses, birth and death certificate requests, assumed name certificates and passport applications. For a seller, the recording department is the one that matters.

The Clerk of Court is Dana Benson. The office phone is (318) 327-1444, and the courthouse is on South Grand Street in Monroe. Wikipedia notes that the parish courthouse in Monroe was built in the 1930s by the contractor George A. Caldwell.

When is the Ouachita Parish Clerk of Court open and how do you pay?

The office is open Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., except legal holidays. The clerk's page lists upcoming closures, including Thanksgiving Day, the Friday after Thanksgiving, Christmas Eve, Christmas Day and New Year's Eve in 2026.

The clerk's page says plainly that no personal checks are accepted by the office. Online accounts and copies are paid by credit card, and the page lists Visa, MasterCard, Discover and American Express. A third-party convenience fee of 3.49 percent applies, with a $1.00 minimum, under La. R.S. 13:841 and Act No. 403.

  • Hours: Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
  • Phone: (318) 327-1444.
  • Personal checks: not accepted.
  • Cards: accepted online with a 3.49 percent fee, $1.00 minimum.
  • Closed on legal holidays listed on the clerk's schedule.

If your closing falls near one of those dates, ask your title company how recording will be timed.

How do you search Ouachita Parish land records online?

Ouachita Parish land records are searched through a Clerk Connect account, which is a paid subscription. The clerk's page says the office merged with one software service company in 2023, covering civil inquiry, criminal inquiry and property records, and added non-support records as of September 1, 2026.

Access optionPrice listed by the clerk
Day rate (24 hours)$20.00
Month rate$75.00
Year rate$800.00
Per page$0.50

Certified copies can also be ordered online. The clerk also promotes a free "eClerks Alert" service that watches land and criminal records across Louisiana parishes.

The clerk's online system is at opclerkofcourt.com. Help with accounts is available by phone at extension 3501.

How do you record a deed in Ouachita Parish?

You record a deed by presenting the signed act of sale to the clerk's recording department, in person or through the clerk's electronic filing system. Most sellers never do this themselves, because the closing attorney or notary files the sale and the mortgage cancellation after signing.

The clerk's rules for electronic filing set out technical standards. Submissions must be PDF files of at least 300 DPI, with plain file names of 50 characters or fewer, no password protection and no embedded video, audio or other PDFs. The rules were adopted on May 12, 2025.

A new state rule also affects attorneys. Under Act No. 352 of the 2025 Regular Session, now part of Code of Civil Procedure Article 253(B)(2) and (3), attorney filings can no longer be faxed or mailed. Effective January 1, 2026 they must be filed in person on paper or sent electronically through a clerk's system or the Louisiana Clerks' Remote Access Authority.

We could not open a current Ouachita Parish recording fee schedule, so no per-page figure is given here. Ask the recording department or your closing attorney for the cost before closing day.

Is there a transfer tax when you sell in Ouachita Parish?

We could not confirm a parish or state transfer tax rate for Ouachita Parish from an official source, so this page does not state one. The closing statement your title company prepares will show every recording charge and any tax that applies to your sale.

Ask for a draft settlement statement several days before closing. It will list recording fees, the mortgage cancellation fee, prorated property tax and any payoff to the Sheriff's Tax Office. Comparing that draft with the clerk's fee page is the simplest way to catch an error.

What liens and tax items does the clerk's record show?

The land records show mortgages, recorded liens and the assessment roll lien that attaches to a property for unpaid property tax. Under La. R.S. 47:1993, once the assessor's roll is delivered to the recorder of mortgages, it acts as a lien and privilege on each property assessed.

That statute says the lien generally ranks ahead of other encumbrances, apart from prior-year rolls and tax lien certificates. A buyer's title examiner will search for exactly these items. If a lien shows up, the seller usually has to pay it off or arrange for it to be paid at closing.

The Ouachita Parish Sheriff collects the tax as ex-officio tax collector, and the Tax Office number is 318-324-2536. The state guide says late taxes accrue 1 percent interest per month, and a tax sale carries a three-year right of redemption for immovable property.

How do Sheriff sales and foreclosures connect to the clerk's records?

Court-ordered seizures of property are handled by the Sheriff's Civil Division, and the sales are posted publicly. The Sheriff's page says the division handles writs of seizure and sale, garnishments, attachments and writs of possession. After advertising in the legal section of a local newspaper, property is sold at public auction.

The page states that sales are held every Wednesday morning at 10:00 a.m. through an online bidding site, under a process that began on July 10, 2024. The same office serves civil papers and carries out evictions on seized and sold property when occupants do not leave as directed.

The Sheriff's page refers to orders from the parish courts and the 4th Judicial District Court. If your house is in or near foreclosure, the recorded seizure and the court record both affect what a buyer can do, so talk to a licensed attorney about timing.

Why does Ouachita Parish geography matter for recording?

Ouachita Parish spans 632 square miles, and Monroe is both its seat and largest city. The clerk's office is at the courthouse in Monroe, but the properties it records can be in West Monroe, Richwood, Sterlington or unincorporated areas such as Calhoun or Swartz.

The clerk in Monroe keeps the records for the whole parish. City and parish taxes can still differ, because the Assessor's FAQ says homestead exemption does not reduce city taxes. Gather the parcel number, last deed and any survey before you list, and the closing will move faster.

More questions about Ouachita Parish, LA Clerk of Court

Where do I record a deed in Ouachita Parish?

Record it with the Ouachita Parish Clerk of Court, whose courthouse is on South Grand Street in Monroe. The phone number is (318) 327-1444, and filings can also go through the clerk's electronic system.

Does the Ouachita Parish Clerk of Court accept personal checks?

No. The clerk's page states that no personal checks are paid to the office. Online accounts and copies use credit cards, with a 3.49 percent convenience fee.

How much does it cost to view Ouachita Parish land records online?

The clerk lists $20 for a day, $75 for a month and $800 for a year, plus $0.50 per page. Credit cards carry a 3.49 percent fee with a $1.00 minimum.

Is there a state transfer tax I must pay as a seller in Ouachita Parish?

We could not confirm one from an official source, so check your settlement statement and ask your closing attorney. Do not rely on this page for a rate.

When does the Ouachita Parish clerk's office close for holidays?

It is closed on legal holidays. The 2026 list on the clerk's page includes Thanksgiving Day, the Friday after, Christmas Eve, Christmas Day and New Year's Eve.

When are Ouachita Parish Sheriff sales held?

They are held every Wednesday at 10:00 a.m. through an online bidding site named on the Sheriff's Civil Division page.

Where does a Washington Parish deed get recorded?

A Washington Parish deed is recorded with the Clerk of Court in Franklinton, who keeps the parish land records. The office is at 908-B Washington St., Franklinton, LA 70438, and the phone number is (985) 839-4663. Mail for public records requests goes to the Custodian of Records at P. O. Box 607, Franklinton, LA 70438.

The clerk's website lists land records as mortgages, conveyances and UCC filings, along with affidavits, oaths and bonds. In Louisiana the person who passes a sale before a notary has a duty to record it. Under La. R.S. 35:199, a notary must record acts of sale of immovable property outside Orleans Parish within fifteen days with the recorder of the parish where the property sits. For a Washington Parish house, that recorder is this office.

The parish seat is Franklinton, but the property does not have to be in town. A house near Bogalusa, Angie, Varnado or Mount Hermon is recorded in the same place. The state's local government page lists Bogalusa as the city, Franklinton as the town, Angie and Varnado as villages, and Mount Hermon as an unincorporated community.

What does the Washington Parish clerk charge to record a sale?

The clerk's posted schedule starts at $120.00 for a general recordation of 1 to 5 pages in one index type. The fee is assessed separately for each recording book, so a sale that goes into the conveyance records and a mortgage that goes into the mortgage records are charged on their own. The page says each tiered fee includes up to 10 names indexed and one certified copy.

That $120.00 figure already contains two built-in charges: a $5.00 Louisiana Clerk Remote Access Authority portal fee under La. R.S. 13:754 and a $15.00 Washington Parish Government Surcharge under La. R.S. 33:1236(55)(a). The schedule is marked as effective August 1, 2017 under Act 173 of that year's session, and the site's home page also records that copy prices rose to $1.00 per page on May 1, 2025.

Is there a transfer tax in Washington Parish?

The clerk's published fee schedule has no transfer tax line, only recording, indexing, certificate, cancellation, copy and similar charges. If you want a firm answer for your own sale, ask the clerk's land records department or your closing notary to confirm the total before closing day.

What the schedule does list is a set of formatting rules that can cost you money if they are missed. Every document filed for recordation must be captioned with the type of act on the first page. It needs a 2-inch top margin and 1-inch bottom and side margins on the first page, and it has to be on 8 1/2 by 11 or 8 1/2 by 14 inch paper with type no smaller than 8 point. A document that misses these rules can draw the $15.00 non-compliance fee.

The clerk also asks that an original and one copy be submitted. The copy is certified and returned in a self-addressed, stamped envelope that the customer supplies. In office the clerk accepts cash, check, money order or credit or debit card. By mail it takes a check or money order only.

What happens to old liens and mortgages when you sell?

Anything recorded against your house stays of record until it is cancelled, so sellers usually clear liens before or at closing. The clerk charges $55.00 for a single cancellation and $75.00 for cancelling a prescribed judgment, bond forfeiture judgment or tax lien, which includes a certificate of the clerk. A duplicate cancellation certificate is $10.00.

Judgments and liens are the items sellers most often discover late. The clerk's schedule includes an affidavit of identity charge of $23.00 for a judgment or lien dated before July 1, 2012, with no charge for one dated after that. That affidavit exists because a name on an old judgment can match a seller's name without being the same person.

A mortgage certificate is the usual way to see what is recorded against a property. The clerk charges $20.00 for one name and one tract. If you want to look yourself, the clerk offers an online records search through Cott Systems, with a 24-hour access option listed at $20.00 and a 30-day option listed at $75.00, plus $1.00 per page to print. Confirm current access prices on the login page before you pay.

  • Pull a mortgage and lien certificate in every name that has owned the house.
  • Ask for cancellations of any paid mortgage that was never released of record.
  • Check for recorded judgments in your name, and know that an affidavit of identity may be needed if the name is a common one.
  • Confirm the property description matches the deed, especially for acreage or a plat larger than 8 1/2 by 14 inches, which carries a separate $125.00 charge.

What is Washington Parish like for a house seller?

Washington Parish is an interior parish roughly 65 miles north of New Orleans on the Mississippi border. Greater New Orleans, Inc. describes it as once a timber and paper hub that now has agriculture, manufacturing, food processing, retail and service businesses. Its profile lists two local airports, in Bogalusa and Franklinton, and six major freight lines.

Bogalusa was founded in 1906 and was built around the Great Southern Lumber Company, according to the city's website. It sits where Bogue Lusa Creek flows into the Pearl River and covers 9.9 square miles with 121 miles of paved streets. International Paper still operates a paper mill and converting plant there, per the mayor's office page. Louisiana Highways 10 and 21 intersect in Bogalusa, and the city says New Orleans is about an hour away via the Lake Pontchartrain Causeway.

Louisiana Economic Development notes that the parish has two business parks and sites with rail and highway access, with easy reach of Interstates 55, 59, 10 and 12.

How do property tax and assessment fit into a Washington Parish sale?

In Louisiana the parish assessor values the property and the clerk only records the paperwork, so the two offices answer different questions. The Washington Parish Assessor's office can be reached at (985) 839-7815, and its website offers assessment search, parcel maps, exemption and re-assessment pages and forms.

The assessor's appeals page explains the path for disputing a value. The assessment lists are open for public inspection for 15 days within a 30-day window between August 15 and September 15, and the assessor publishes in the local paper which two weeks apply. A taxpayer who disagrees fills out the Notice of Appeal Request for Board of Review (form 3101) and schedules a hearing with the parish Board of Review. If either side is unhappy with the result, the Board can supply Form 3103.A for review by the Louisiana Tax Commission.

If you are selling an inherited house, the clerk's civil department handles succession, probate and tutorships, so the judgment of possession that proves your right to sell is filed with the same office that records the deed. Louisiana has not adopted transfer-on-death deeds for real property, according to one Louisiana succession law firm's library page, so heirs often have to go through a succession first.

What should a Washington Parish seller check before closing?

Start with the record, then the property, then the paper. A short checklist helps because Louisiana sales must be passed before a notary and then recorded in the right parish within the time the statute sets.

  • Confirm the recording parish. A parcel is recorded where it sits, not where the owner lives.
  • Order a mortgage and lien certificate and read every item on it.
  • Gather cancellation documents for paid-off loans so they can be recorded.
  • Check that the act of sale is formatted to the clerk's margin, caption and paper rules.
  • Ask whether the clerk or your notary will e-record. The clerk's site points customers to e-recording partners on its online services page.
  • Look up the assessment on the assessor's search page so you know what the parish has on file.

If the house needs work, has a tenant or came through an estate, a cash buyer can close on terms that skip the repair list. We buy as-is in Washington Parish, and the recording steps above still apply to any buyer, so the clerk's fees are worth knowing either way.
